name: ज्ञानविज्ञानयोग
meaning: The Yoga of Knowledge and Realisation
teaching: Krishna begins to speak of himself: the taste in water, the light in the moon and sun, the thread on which all worlds are strung like pearls. The divine is not elsewhere — it is the essence inside every essence. Few seek this; of the four kinds who turn to God, the one who seeks knowing itself is dearest, for that one seeks nothing in return. The Teacher turns the lamp on Himself: two natures, one thread through all pearls, a veil divine and crossable only by refuge. Four kinds of seekers arrive; the rarest says — Vasudeva is everything.
questions: When you pray or aspire, which of the four are you — the distressed, the seeker of gain, the curious, or the one who simply wants to know?
Can you taste water today and notice what the taste itself is?
What 'deity' — career, approval, security — do you worship for limited fruit?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
मय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः ।
असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु॥
verses.transliteration:
mayyāsaktamanāḥ pārtha yogaṃ yuñjanmadāśrayaḥ
asaṃśayaṃ samagraṃ māṃ yathā jñāsyasi tacchṛṇu
verses.essence: With mind attached to me, practicing yoga with me as refuge — hear how you shall know me wholly, beyond doubt.
verses.translation: O Arjuna, hear how you shall without doubt know Me fully, with the mind intent on Me, practising Yoga and taking refuge in Me.

anvaya.parts: आसक्त (attached, fixed) + मनस् (mind): one whose mind is fixed on something

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while doing)

anvaya.parts: मद् (me) + आश्रय (refuge, support): one whose refuge is me
अ (not) + संशय (doubt): without doubt

verses.explanation: A new movement opens: the first six chapters taught the self; the next six will teach the One the self meets. The conditions are intimacy itself — mind attached *to me*, refuge *in me* — and the promise is audacious: samagram, knowing the Infinite *wholly*, with doubt gone. Attachment, the great enemy so far, is rehabilitated when its object is the Divine.
verses.connection: Picks up exactly where 6.47 left the crown — with the most-yoked lover of God — and begins teaching what the beloved is.
verses.reflection: Practice today with mind attached to the highest and refuge actually taken — and expect to know, not guess.
verses.background: Chapter 7 opens with Krishna speaking unasked, having just ended chapter 6 by praising the yogi who worships him with an absorbed mind. Śrīdhara notes the question this leaves open: what kind of being is the one to be worshipped? Krishna begins to describe himself, first inviting Arjuna to listen.
verses.hook: How can you come to know God completely, without any doubt?

views.text: Taking refuge in Me means rejecting every other means: where others resort to rites, austerity or charity for their ends, this yogi relies on the Lord alone. 'Fully' means knowing Him with all His powers and glories.
The mind is bound to the Lord by overwhelming love, so deeply that it would fall apart the moment it lost touch with His nature, qualities and deeds.
The truth of the self, with its yoga, has been taught; now the teaching turns to the Lord's own nature, the one to be worshipped; 'fully' means together with His powers, strength and lordship.
Having called the devoted yogi the best, Krishna, unasked, begins to explain how God is known, asking Arjun to listen closely with a mind fixed on him.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञानं तेऽहं सविज्ञानमिदं वक्ष्याम्यशेषतः ।
यज्ज्ञात्वा नेह भूयोऽन्यज्ज्ञातव्यमवशिष्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
jñānaṃ te'haṃ savijñānamidaṃ vakṣyāmyaśeṣataḥ
yajjñātvā neha bhūyo'nyajjñātavyamavaśiṣyate
verses.essence: I shall teach you this knowledge together with realization, knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
verses.translation: I shall declare to thee in full this knowledge combined with realisation, after knowing which nothing more here remains to be known.

anvaya.parts: स (with) + विज्ञान (realized, distinguishing knowledge): knowledge joined with realization
अ (without) + शेष (remainder): leaving nothing out

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (object of 'having known')
gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (what must be known)

verses.explanation: Two knowings promised as a pair: jñāna, the understanding that can be taught, and vijñāna, the direct taste that can only be had. And then the largest claim in epistemology: after this, nothing else *needs* knowing — because to know the root is to implicitly hold every branch. All other knowledge is regional; this one is of the territory itself.
verses.connection: Sets the stakes for the chapter: not another doctrine, but the knowledge that retires the search.
verses.reflection: Seek the knowledge that ends seeking: ask today not for more facts but for the root of facts.
verses.background: Having asked Arjuna to listen, Krishna now describes the teaching he is about to give, before giving any of it. Śaṅkara reads it as praise of the coming teaching, meant to draw the hearer's full attention.
verses.hook: What knowledge is so complete that nothing else remains to be known?

refs.note: Through bhakti Vyasa fixed his pure mind on God and saw the Supreme Person with his Maya under his control, showing realized knowledge comes through devotion.

views.text: Vijñāna is personal enlightenment, direct experience added to understanding; the Lord praises this knowledge to win the hearer's attention, since whoever knows Him truly becomes, in effect, all-knowing.
Vijñāna is distinguishing knowledge: knowing the Lord as set apart from everything, animate and inanimate, as the one opposed to all evil and full of countless auspicious qualities.
Jñāna and vijñāna are taken as knowledge and action; nothing lies outside these two, since everything knowable is rooted in knowing and doing.
Jñāna is the indirect knowledge gained from scripture; vijñāna is direct realization of the Self. Know the Self and everything is known, as Śaunaka asked of Aṅgiras.

Theoretical knowledge from the Guru must ripen through practice into direct realization, like tasting honey rather than hearing of it; Krishna promises Arjun both, after which nothing remains to know.

verses.devanagari:
मनुष्याणां सहस्रेषु कश्चिद्यतति सिद्धये ।
यततामपि सिद्धानां कश्चिन्मां वेत्ति तत्त्वतः॥
verses.transliteration:
manuṣyāṇāṃ sahasreṣu kaścidyatati siddhaye
yatatāmapi siddhānāṃ kaścinmāṃ vetti tattvataḥ
verses.essence: Among thousands of humans, scarcely one strives for perfection; and of those who strive and succeed, scarcely one knows me in truth.
verses.translation: Among thousands of men, one perchance strives for perfection; even among those successful strivers, only one perchance knows Me in essence.

anvaya.form: past participle used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)

verses.explanation: A double filter, stated without flattery: among thousands, rare is the one who even begins; and among those striving ones, rarer still is the one who knows *him* as he is, tattvataḥ. The arithmetic is not meant to discourage but to locate Arjuna: he is being handed, mid-battlefield, what the rarest seekers spend lifetimes approaching. Kaścid yatati siddhaye: the striving itself already sets one among the thousands' exceptions. The rarity is a measure of the effort the knowledge asks, not a closed door: the earnest seeker who keeps going is exactly the one the verse is counting.
verses.connection: Prices the gift of 7.1–2 — and makes its free offering to Arjuna the more astonishing.
verses.reflection: Let the rarity sober you sweetly: among thousands, one seeks. You are reading this — continue.
verses.background: Krishna has just promised knowledge that leaves nothing more to know. Śaṅkara reasons that knowledge with so great a result must be hard to reach, and asks how so. This verse answers by measuring how few people even set out, before the teaching itself begins.
verses.hook: How many people who seek perfection actually come to know God as he is?

views.text: Perfection here is the rise of knowledge through a purified mind; those who strive for liberation are already counted as 'perfected', yet only one of them knows the Lord in truth.
Reads three tiers of rarity: few strive, fewer know Him, fewest know Him as He truly is, distinguished from all else. It looks ahead to 7.19's 'very hard to find'.
Without devotion to Me, knowledge of Me is hard to get: even among those who know the self, only one knows the Supreme Self in truth, and that by My grace.
Few humans strive for perfection, and fewer still know God in truth, because without loving devotion no path, whether action, knowledge or hatha yoga, reveals him beyond mere theory.

verses.devanagari:
भूमिरापोऽनलो वायुः खं मनो बुद्धिरेव च ।
अहंकार इतीयं मे भिन्ना प्रकृतिरष्टधा॥
verses.transliteration:
bhūmirāpo'nalo vāyuḥ khaṃ mano buddhireva ca
ahaṃkāra itīyaṃ me bhinnā prakṛtiraṣṭadhā
verses.essence: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, understanding and ego — this is my nature, divided eightfold.
verses.translation: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect and egoism thus is My Nature divided eightfold.

anvaya.parts: अहम् (I) + कार (making): the 'I-maker'

verses.explanation: The inventory of everything science can touch: five elements ascending in subtlety, then the three instruments of inner life — mind, intellect, the very sense of 'I'. All eight, including the ego that feels most like *me*, are classed as prakṛti: his equipment, his lower nature. The self one ordinarily identifies with is here itemized as machinery.
verses.connection: Begins the chapter's metaphysics: the visible and mental world catalogued as the lower of two natures.
verses.reflection: Name the eight today: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego. Notice each one as nature at work in you.
verses.background: With the listener now attentive, Śrīdhara explains, Krishna starts to show how he creates the world through his nature. He divides that nature into a lower and a higher kind; this verse lists the eight parts of the lower one, from the elements to mind, intellect and the sense of 'I'.
verses.hook: What are the eight parts of the material nature Krishna calls his own?

refs.note: Describes creation unfolding in sequence from space to air, fire, water, earth, plants, food and the human being, matching the verse's elements as one energy of God.

views.text: This prakṛti is the Lord's power called māyā, not the Sāṅkhya pradhāna. The elements are the subtle ones; mind stands for ego, intellect for mahat, and ego for the Unmanifest steeped in ignorance.
Prakṛti is the material cause of a universe of objects, means and places of enjoyment, divided into these eight substances, and all of it belongs to the Lord.
The eight are one nature, so the universe is unitary, made of a single material cause; monism is shown even while using the language of prakṛti.
Matter, including mind, intellect and ego, is a single energy of God, Maya, unfolding through subtle stages into the five elements; he finds in this a unified account older than modern physics.

verses.devanagari:
अपरेयमितस्त्वन्यां प्रकृतिं विद्धि मे पराम् ।
जीवभूतां महाबाहो ययेदं धार्यते जगत्॥
verses.transliteration:
apareyamitastvanyāṃ prakṛtiṃ viddhi me parām
jīvabhūtāṃ mahābāho yayedaṃ dhāryate jagat
verses.essence: This is the lower. Know my other, higher nature, Mahabaho — the life-element by which this universe is upheld.
verses.translation: This is the inferior Prakriti, O mighty-armed (Arjuna); know thou as different from it My higher Prakriti (Nature), the very life-element, by which this world is upheld.

anvaya.meaning: which has become the living souls
anvaya.parts: जीव (living being, soul) + भूत (become): that which has become the jīva
महत् (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty

anvaya.form: verb, present, passive, 3rd person singular (is being done)

verses.explanation: The hierarchy revealed: everything in 7.4, galaxies, thoughts, the ego itself, is aparā, lower; above it stands the parā prakṛti, the conscious life-principle, jīva-bhūtā, which has become every living soul. Matter does not hold itself up: yayedaṃ dhāryate jagat, it is by this conscious nature that the world is upheld. Each living being is a strand of the Divine's *higher* nature, the world's true infrastructure.
verses.connection: Completes 7.4's picture: two natures, one Lord — and the reader belongs to the higher one.
verses.reflection: Feel the higher nature in you this hour: the aliveness that uses the equipment of 7.4.
verses.background: Krishna has just listed the eight parts of his nature: the five elements, mind, intellect and ego. He now closes that list by giving it a rank and points to a second nature of his, beyond the eight, the conscious life that holds the world together.
verses.hook: Beyond matter, what higher energy of God sustains the living world?

refs.note: As fire in one place spreads its light everywhere, the one Supreme pervades the whole world through his energy, matching souls as God's energy.
Teaches that the soul is God's energy and Krishna the energetic, the relationship this verse sets out.

views.text: The lower nature is impure and binding; the higher is pure, 'essentially Myself', the knower of the field, which has taken the form of individual souls and upholds the world by pervading it.
The higher prakṛti is the individual self, different in kind from inanimate matter, which exists for the enjoyment of conscious beings; through the selves the whole inanimate world is sustained.
The same prakṛti that became the eight has also become the personal soul, so it is two-fold, knowable and knower, yet belongs to the Lord alone and never leaves Him.
Souls are God's superior spiritual energy, distinct from matter. Since energy is both one with and different from its source, the soul is neither God himself nor wholly separate from him.

verses.devanagari:
एतद्योनीनि भूतानि सर्वाणीत्युपधारय ।
अहं कृत्स्नस्य जगतः प्रभवः प्रलयस्तथा॥
verses.transliteration:
etadyonīni bhūtāni sarvāṇītyupadhāraya
ahaṃ kṛtsnasya jagataḥ prabhavaḥ pralayastathā
verses.essence: Know all beings to have these two as their womb. I am the origin of the entire universe, and likewise its dissolution.
verses.translation: Know that these two (Natures) are the womb of all beings. So I am the source and dissolution of the whole universe.

anvaya.meaning: having these two as their source
anvaya.form: adjective (compound), neuter, nominative plural (within the 'thus' clause)
anvaya.parts: एतद् (these) + योनि (womb, source): things whose womb is these two natures

verses.explanation: The two natures meet, and everything alive is their offspring: matter shaped into bodies, conscious life entering them, both natures together the womb of every being, and both belonging to one owner. So the conclusion follows like arithmetic: prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ, I am where all this comes from and where it folds back. Source and sea, both him.
verses.connection: Joins 7.4–5 into a single cosmology with one proprietor at both ends.
verses.reflection: Trace one thing today to its double origin — matter shaped, consciousness witnessing — and bow to both.
verses.background: Two natures of Krishna have now been described: the eightfold material one and the higher one that is life itself. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as showing that these two are the sources of all things, and that through them Krishna is the cause of the world's coming and going.
verses.hook: Where do all living beings come from, and where do they return?

views.text: The two natures are the field and the knower of the field; since they are the cause of all things, the omniscient Lord is, through them, the origin and end of the universe.
Every being from Brahmā to a blade of grass is a mix of self and matter born of these two natures; because they arise from Him, the Lord is the origin, dissolution and owner of all.
The inert nature turns into bodies; the conscious nature, a portion of Me, enters them as the enjoyer and sustains them by its own karma. Both arise from Me, so I am the supreme cause.
Every living being joins God's two energies, matter and soul; at dissolution all creation and unliberated souls rest in Maha Vishnu, so God is source, sustainer and resting place of everything.

verses.devanagari:
मत्तः परतरं नान्यत्किञ्चिदस्ति धनञ्जय ।
मयि सर्वमिदं प्रोतं सूत्रे मणिगणा इव॥
verses.transliteration:
mattaḥ parataraṃ nānyatkiñcidasti dhanañjaya
mayi sarvamidaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇigaṇā iva
verses.essence: There is nothing whatever higher than me, Dhananjaya. All this is strung on me like pearls on a thread.
verses.translation: There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Arjuna. All this is strung on Me, as clusters of gems on a string.

anvaya.parts: धन (wealth) + जय (winning): one who wins wealth

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, nominative singular (subject)
past participle, neuter, nominative singular (has been done)

anvaya.parts: मणि (gem, pearl) + गण (group): rows of gems

verses.explanation: First the flat absolute, mattaḥ parataraṃ nānyat, nothing whatever higher than me; then the image that softens it into intimacy: pearls on a thread. The thread runs through every pearl, unseen, giving the scattered beads their unity and their hang; remove it and the necklace is a handful of debris. The world's coherence *is* the hidden God within it. Rāmānuja reads the thread as the Lord abiding as the Self of the world, which is His body; but every reading wears the same necklace: whatever you handle, you are handling something strung on God.
verses.connection: Crowns 7.6's cosmology with the chapter's master-image — immanence as the invisible string.
verses.reflection: Look along one ordinary object today until you sense the thread it is strung on.
verses.background: Having called himself the origin and end of the whole universe through his two natures, Krishna draws the consequence. Śrīdhara explains that this verse adds his role in keeping the world in being, and Krishna gives it the image of a string running through a necklace.
verses.hook: Is there anything higher than Krishna, and how does the world hang on him?

refs.note: States that nothing is equal to God or greater than him and that his powers are manifold, echoing Krishna's claim that nothing is higher.
Brahma praises Krishna as the eternal Supreme Lord, the beginningless origin and cause of all causes, supporting the reading that Krishna himself is the Supreme.

views.text: Nothing else is the cause of the world; the Lord alone is its source, and all things are woven on Him like cloth on its warp, or pearls on a string.

The Lord is supreme as cause and master of both natures and as possessor of infinite qualities. All things are strung on Him as their Self; they are His body and modes, so all words finally denote Him.
As the string runs unseen inside the necklace, the Lord stays immanent in all; though spoken of as distinct from prakṛti and soul, He leaves no room for Sāṅkhya-Yoga dualism.

God is the thread on which creation is strung; souls move freely like beads yet depend on him. By saying 'I', Krishna shows his own personal form is the ultimate Truth, with no higher formless source.

verses.devanagari:
रसोऽहमप्सु कौन्तेय प्रभास्मि शशिसूर्ययोः ।
प्रणवः सर्ववेदेषु शब्दः खे पौरुषं नृषु॥
verses.transliteration:
raso'hamapsu kaunteya prabhāsmi śaśisūryayoḥ
praṇavaḥ sarvavedeṣu śabdaḥ khe pauruṣaṃ nṛṣu
verses.essence: I am the taste in water, Kaunteya, the radiance of moon and sun, the Om in all the Vedas, the sound in ether, the prowess in men.
verses.translation: I am the sapidity in water, O Arjuna; I am the light in the moon and the sun; I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, sound in ether and virility in men.

anvaya.meaning: of the moon and the sun
anvaya.form: noun (compound), masculine, genitive dual (of the two)
anvaya.parts: शशिन् (moon, 'hare-marked') + सूर्य (sun): the moon and the sun as a pair
सर्व (all) + वेद (Veda): all the Vedas

verses.explanation: The thread of 7.7 located, sense by sense: in each thing, its essence — not water but its taste, not the sun but its shining, not scripture but its seed-syllable. The hunt for God is redirected from elsewhere to *deeper here*: take any experience, find what makes it most itself, and you are touching the string.
verses.connection: Begins the immanence litany (7.8–11): where exactly the pearls touch the thread.
verses.reflection: Taste water once today as taste itself — the nearest daily sacrament, hiding in the glass.
verses.background: Krishna has said all things are strung on him like gems on a thread. Śaṅkara raises the question this invites: through which qualities is everything strung on him? Krishna begins to answer with examples taken from water, sun and moon, the Vedas, space and human beings.
verses.hook: Where can you find Krishna in water, light, sound and human strength?

views.text: In each case the Lord is the essence on which the thing depends: water rests on Him as its taste, the Vedas on Him as Om, space on Him as sound, men on Him as manhood.
All these, with their special traits, are born from the Lord and exist in Him as His body; He alone truly exists, and they are His modes.
The sound in space is read as the unstruck (anāhata) sound in the inner space of the heart, known to attentive yogins and pervading all the Vedas; that sound is the Absolute.
Sustenance is spelled out: as the subtle element of taste He supports water; Om is the root of all spoken Veda; manliness is effort, since people stand on effort.
God is present in every modification of his energies: the taste water carries, the light of sun and moon, Om in the Vedas, sound in space, and every human ability.

verses.devanagari:
पुण्यो गन्धः पृथिव्यां च तेजश्चास्मि विभावसौ ।
जीवनं सर्वभूतेषु तपश्चास्मि तपस्विषु॥
verses.transliteration:
puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛthivyāṃ ca tejaścāsmi vibhāvasau
jīvanaṃ sarvabhūteṣu tapaścāsmi tapasviṣu
verses.essence: I am the pure fragrance in earth and the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics.
verses.translation: I am the sweet fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in the fire, the life in all beings, and I am the austerity in ascetics.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being): all beings

verses.explanation: The litany deepens from qualities to powers: the scent that rises from rained-on earth, fire's heat-light, and then two that stop the breath — jīvanam, the sheer aliveness in everything alive, and tapas, the very intensity of the striver's striving. Even the effort to reach him is made of him.
verses.connection: Continues 7.8: the seeker discovers the sought inside the seeking itself.
verses.reflection: Catch the fragrance of earth, the heat of fire, your own aliveness — and address each one correctly.
verses.background: Krishna continues the list he began in the previous verse, of the places where he is present in things. After water, the lights of the sky, the Vedas, space and human strength, this verse turns to earth, fire, all living beings and those who practise austerity.
verses.hook: What in earth, fire, living beings and ascetics does Krishna say he is?

views.text: Pure fragrance is earth's natural smell; foulness comes from contact with other things, owing to people's ignorance and impurity. Life is that by which all creatures live.
Earth's smell is pure by its own nature; foulness and excess come from mixture with the other elements.
As odour, life and austerity, the Lord is the support of everything, and the power that helps ascetics master mind and senses. Had Arjuna asked who the foul smell is, the answer would be: also I.
God is the vital essence of everything on earth: the fragrance of soil, the brightness of flame, the life of all creatures, and even the power behind an ascetic's penance.

verses.devanagari:
बीजं मां सर्वभूतानां विद्धि पार्थ सनातनम् ।
बुद्धिर्बुद्धिमतामस्मि तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
bījaṃ māṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ viddhi pārtha sanātanam
buddhirbuddhimatāmasmi tejastejasvināmaham
verses.essence: Know me, Partha, as the eternal seed of all beings; I am the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendor of the splendid.
verses.translation: Know Me, O Arjuna, as the eternal seed of all beings; I am the intelligence of the intelligent; the splendour of the splendid objects am I.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, accusative singular (what you know me as)

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being): all beings

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)
adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)

verses.explanation: Bīja sanātanam — the seed that is eternal: not one ancestor among others but the unspent origin present in every generation. Then the pattern sharpens into a formula the chapter will repeat: of any excellence, he is the excellence itself — the brightness *of* the bright, the sharpness *of* the sharp mind reading this.
verses.connection: Extends the litany from elements to capacities — God as the genius inside genius.
verses.reflection: When you meet brilliance today, in yourself or another, silently return the loan to its source.
verses.background: The list of Krishna's presence in things goes on. Having named qualities of the elements and of living beings, he now speaks of the ongoing seed from which beings arise, and of the qualities that mark out the gifted: intelligence in the intelligent, brilliance in the brilliant.
verses.hook: What is the original seed from which every being comes?

views.text: The seed is the source of growth of all beings; intellect is the mind's power of discrimination, and tejas here is courage, the boldness of the bold.
The eternal seed is the power in every species to produce its own kind, running through every generation, not the individual seed that perishes with each plant.
Seed means cause. Had Arjuna asked for the Lord's own seed, the answer would be: there is none; He is the causeless Cause.
As every cause is the seed of its effect, God is the eternal seed of all beings, and outstanding intelligence or brilliance in anyone is his grace working through them.

verses.devanagari:
बलं बलवतां चाहं कामरागविवर्जितम् ।
धर्माविरुद्धो भूतेषु कामोऽस्मि भरतर्षभ॥
verses.transliteration:
balaṃ balavatāṃ cāhaṃ kāmarāgavivarjitam
dharmāviruddho bhūteṣu kāmo'smi bharatarṣabha
verses.essence: I am the strength of the strong, free of craving and passion; in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma, Bharatarshabha.
verses.translation: Of the strong, I am the strength devoid of desire and attachment, and in (all) beings, I am the desire unopposed to Dharma, O Arjuna.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)

anvaya.base: काम-राग-विवर्जित · free from craving and clinging
anvaya.parts: काम (craving) + राग (attachment) + विवर्जित (free of): free from craving and attachment

anvaya.base: धर्म-अविरुद्ध · not in conflict with dharma
anvaya.parts: धर्म (right order, duty) + अविरुद्ध (not opposed): in keeping with dharma
भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull): the finest of the Bharatas

verses.explanation: The litany's most surprising line: kāma, desire itself, the enemy of chapter 3, claimed by God, with one qualifier: dharmāviruddha, not opposed to dharma. The commentators keep the claim narrow and practical: the wanting that keeps a body fed and sound, the desire that stays within one's own duty, the strength that serves without craving or clinging. Such desire is not a tolerated weakness but a divine presence. The Gita does not condemn wanting as such; it disowns wanting that breaks loose from dharma.
verses.connection: Completes 7.8–11 by reclaiming even desire — the chapter's quiet rehabilitation of the human.
verses.reflection: Honor one desire today that runs within dharma — wanting rightly is also His face.
verses.background: This verse ends the run of examples Krishna began with the taste in water. It turns to strength and to desire, the two most easily misused powers in a person, and names the kind of each that belongs to him.
verses.hook: What kind of strength and desire does Krishna identify with himself?

views.text: Kāma is hankering for what is not yet had, rāga is fondness for what is had; the Lord is the strength free of both, needed only to maintain the body, and the desire for food and drink that scripture allows.
Desire here is the Will, pure consciousness and the Lord's own energy, present in every object and opposed to none; reading it as permission to enjoy the three aims together is rejected.
Strength free of rajasic craving and tamasic thirst is the sattvic capacity to do one's own duty; desire not opposed to dharma is desire for one's own spouse for the sake of children.
God is the serene strength that lets people do their duty, free of craving and attachment, and desire kept within dharma, such as a householder's regulated union for procreation.

verses.devanagari:
ये चैव सात्त्विका भावा राजसास्तामसाश्च ये ।
मत्त एवेति तान्विद्धि न त्वहं तेषु ते मयि॥
verses.transliteration:
ye caiva sāttvikā bhāvā rājasāstāmasāśca ye
matta eveti tānviddhi na tvahaṃ teṣu te mayi
verses.essence: Whatever states there are — of sattva, of rajas, of tamas — know them as from me alone. I am not in them; they are in me.
verses.translation: Whatever beings (and objects) that are pure, active and inert, know that they proceed from Me. They are in Me, yet I am not in them.
verses.explanation: Total sourcing with a precise asymmetry: every mood and mode the three gunas weave, luminous, driven, dull, issues from him; yet he is not *contained* in them, while they are contained in him. Every wave rises from the ocean; no wave holds the ocean. The formula prevents both errors: a God absent from the world, and a God reducible to it.
verses.connection: Wraps the immanence verses with their safeguard — presence without imprisonment.
verses.reflection: Whatever state arises in you today — bright, restless, dull — file it: from Him, contained in Him.
verses.background: Having given particular examples of his presence, Krishna now sums them all up. He brings in every state of mind and being that arises from the three qualities of nature, calm, restless or dull, and states how they relate to him.
verses.hook: If everything comes from God, is God then contained in things?

views.text: 'I am not in them' means I am not subject to them or under their control, as transmigrating beings are; they are in Me, under My control.
They abide in Me as My body, but I never depend on them; unlike a soul served by its body, I gain nothing from them. They exist only for My play.
They depend on the Lord as the imagined snake depends on the rope: the snake is in the rope, but the rope is never in the snake.
All states, good, bad or ugly, are made possible by God's energy, yet he stays independent of his creation and beyond it.

verses.devanagari:
त्रिभिर्गुणमयैर्भावैरेभिः सर्वमिदं जगत् ।
मोहितं नाभिजानाति मामेभ्यः परमव्ययम्॥
verses.transliteration:
tribhirguṇamayairbhāvairebhiḥ sarvamidaṃ jagat
mohitaṃ nābhijānāti māmebhyaḥ paramavyayam
verses.essence: Deluded by these three states made of the gunas, this whole world does not recognize me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
verses.translation: Deluded by these Natures (states or things) composed of the three qualities of Nature all this world does not know Me as distinct from them and immutable.

anvaya.parts: गुण (strand, quality) + मय (made of): consisting of the three strands

anvaya.form: past participle, neuter, nominative singular (has been done)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + व्यय (decay, loss): not subject to decay

verses.explanation: The diagnosis of the world's blindness: the gunas are a weather so continuous it is mistaken for the sky. Attention, captured by the three-colored play, never asks what the play is projected on. He is not hidden far away but hidden in plain depth — param, just beyond the moods, exactly where no one looks.
verses.connection: Explains 7.3's rarity: the veil is woven of the very states everyone lives inside.
verses.reflection: Notice the lens at work once today: the gunas showing you everything except what stands behind them.
verses.background: Krishna has shown himself present in everything and the source of every state of being. Śrīdhara voices the question this raises: if you are such a Lord, why do people not know you? This verse gives the cause of the world's failure to recognise him.
verses.hook: Why does most of the world fail to recognize God?

views.text: The three states are attachment, aversion and delusion, transformations of the guṇas, which rob the world of discrimination; the Lord is distinct from them and free of all six changes beginning with birth.
Beings mistake inferior, passing things for enjoyable while the Lord, boundless bliss and the very source of their enjoyableness, goes unknown.
The guṇas come from the Lord, not He from them; one established in identity with Him sees all objects as Him, while one lost in the variety of objects misses His reality.
The three modes of Maya veil consciousness and fascinate souls with passing pleasures; Maya hides God from those turned away from him and troubles them until they turn toward him.

verses.devanagari:
दैवी ह्येषा गुणमयी मम माया दुरत्यया ।
मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते मायामेतां तरन्ति ते॥
verses.transliteration:
daivī hyeṣā guṇamayī mama māyā duratyayā
māmeva ye prapadyante māyāmetāṃ taranti te
verses.essence: For this divine maya of mine, made of the gunas, is hard to cross. Those who take refuge in me alone pass beyond this maya.
verses.translation: Verily, this divine illusion of Mine, made up of the (three) qualities (of Nature) is difficult to cross over; those who take refuge in Me alone, cross over this illusion.

anvaya.parts: गुण (strand, quality) + मय (made of): consisting of the three strands
दुर् (hard) + अत्यय (going beyond): hard to pass beyond

anvaya.base: प्र + √पद् · to go to, resort to

verses.explanation: The veil of 7.13 is named and given an owner: mama māyā, *my* māyā, daivī, divine, not a cosmic accident or a rival power but his own power of enchantment. Hence the futility of fighting it head-on: duratyayā, no technique storms the magician's spell unaided. The single exit is stated with surgical economy: mām eva ye prapadyante, go past the spell by going to the one who casts it. The weaver can part what no one else can tear.
verses.connection: Answers 7.13's predicament: the door through the veil is surrender to its weaver.
verses.reflection: When the veil proves uncrossable today, stop climbing and try the door: refuge, simply taken.
verses.background: Krishna has said the world is deluded by states made of the three qualities of nature. Śrīdhara asks: who, then, does know you? Krishna names how hard this power of illusion is to cross, and the one way across.
verses.hook: How can anyone get past God's divine power of illusion, so hard to cross?

refs.note: Teaches that Maya is nature, God's energy, and God its master, so Maya is real and under him, not mere illusion.
Says some think Maya unreal, but it is in fact a servant of God, supporting that it yields only to his command.

views.text: Refuge is in the Lord as the master of māyā and as one's own Self, giving up all other rites and duties; such people are freed from the bondage of the world.
Māyā is not 'false': like a magician's real power, it is the Lord's real prakṛti of three guṇas, made for His play, which hides Him and makes objects seem enjoyable.
Daivī comes from deva, 'one who plays': this is His play, by which the guṇas, not really different from pure consciousness, appear different; those who see the universe as one with Brahman cross it.
'Me alone' means unwavering devotion: those who worship with such devotion cross even this hard-to-cross māyā, and then they know Me.
Maya is God's real energy, not an illusion, so no self-effort defeats it; only on surrender does God, like a master calling off his guard dog, order Maya to release the soul.

verses.devanagari:
न मां दुष्कृतिनो मूढाः प्रपद्यन्ते नराधमाः ।
माययापहृतज्ञाना आसुरं भावमाश्रिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
na māṃ duṣkṛtino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ
māyayāpahṛtajñānā āsuraṃ bhāvamāśritāḥ
verses.essence: Evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men do not take refuge in me — their discernment stolen by maya, clinging to a demonic mode of being.
verses.translation: The evil-doers and the deluded who are the lowest of men do not seek Me; they whose knowledge is destroyed by illusion follow the ways of demons.

anvaya.parts: दुस् (bad) + कृतिन् (doer): one whose deeds are evil

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine, nominative plural

anvaya.base: प्र + √पद् · to go to, resort to

anvaya.parts: नर (man) + अधम (lowest): the lowest among men
अपहृत (carried off) + ज्ञान (knowledge): those whose knowledge has been taken away

anvaya.base: आ + √श्रि · to lean on, resort to

verses.explanation: If the door is open and simple, why is it not crowded? Four declines, really one: māyayāpahṛta-jñānāḥ — the very faculty that would seek the door has been pickpocketed by the enchantment. The āsura mode is not horns and fangs; it is the settled conviction that grabbing is wiser than offering, which makes surrender look like the one absurd move.
verses.connection: The shadow side of 7.14's promise: who declines the crossing, and what declined in them first.
verses.reflection: Check where cleverness in you serves the wrong master — intelligence stolen is the subtlest theft.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that those who take refuge in him alone cross his illusion. Śaṅkara poses the objection that follows: then why does not everyone take refuge in him? This verse answers by describing the people who do not.
verses.hook: Who are the people who do not take refuge in God?

views.text: The foolish sinners, lowest of men, whose wisdom Māyā has despoiled and who turn to demoniacal ways such as cruelty and untruthfulness, do not take refuge in the supreme God.

Four grades of evil-doers: the foolish, who think themselves independent owners; the lowest, who know Him but will not turn; those whose knowledge is argued away; and the demonic, who know Him and hate Him.

The epithets form a chain of causes: they are lowest because deluded, deluded because sinful, and so māyā takes away even the knowledge they got from scripture and teacher, leaving the demonic nature of chapter 16.
The demonic take the body for the Self, like Virocana, and worship it with fine food and clothes; ignorance is the root of all these evils.
Four kinds do not surrender: the ignorant who have never heard of the goal, the lazy who know but do not act, the proud whose intellect rejects scripture, and the demonic who oppose God.

verses.devanagari:
चतुर्विधा भजन्ते मां जनाः सुकृतिनोऽर्जुन ।
आर्तो जिज्ञासुरर्थार्थी ज्ञानी च भरतर्षभ॥
verses.transliteration:
caturvidhā bhajante māṃ janāḥ sukṛtino'rjuna
ārto jijñāsurarthārthī jñānī ca bharatarṣabha
verses.essence: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower.
verses.translation: Four kinds of virtuous men worship Me, O Arjuna, and they are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth and the wise, O lord of the Bharatas.

anvaya.parts: चतुर् (four) + विधा (kind): of four kinds
सु (good) + कृतिन् (doer): those whose deeds are good

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: अर्थ (wealth, gain) + अर्थिन् (seeker): one who seeks wealth
भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull): the finest of the Bharatas

verses.explanation: A census of the world's prayers, conducted without contempt: the ārta who comes bleeding, the jijñāsu who comes wondering, the arthārthī who comes wanting, and the jñānī who comes for nothing, having found. All four are sukṛtinaḥ, *virtuous*: even the bargaining prayer turned toward him is credited as turning. Motives are graded in the next verse, but admitted here. Whatever first turns the face counts, and devotion, once begun, purifies the motive that began it. The door does not interview the knock.
verses.connection: Maps who does walk through 7.14's door — every motive admitted at its own depth.
verses.reflection: Whichever of the four you are today — hurting, curious, needing, knowing — come anyway. All four count.
verses.background: Having described those who never turn to him, Krishna turns to those who do. Śrīdhara introduces them as people of good deeds in earlier lives, who come in four kinds according to the degree of that merit.
verses.hook: What different reasons bring good people to worship God?

views.text: The afflicted are those overwhelmed by thieves, tigers or disease; the seeker wants to know the Lord's reality; the man of knowledge already knows the reality of Viṣṇu.

The four rise by merit and knowledge: the distressed wants lost wealth back, the wealth-seeker wants new wealth (little difference), the inquirer seeks the self as distinct from matter, and the knower seeks the Lord Himself.
All four worship because of merit from past births; without it the same sufferer would worship petty deities and keep wandering in saṃsāra.
Draupadī and Gajendra prayed in distress, Janaka and Uddhava as inquirers, Dhruva and Sugrīva for gain, Śuka as a knower: be devoted whatever the motive, and devotion will purify it.
Four kinds turn to God: the distressed, as Draupadi did when all other help failed; the curious seeker of knowledge; the seeker of gain, like Dhruv; and the wise who know they belong to God.

verses.devanagari:
तेषां ज्ञानी नित्ययुक्त एकभक्तिर्विशिष्यते ।
प्रियो हि ज्ञानिनोऽत्यर्थमहं स च मम प्रियः॥
verses.transliteration:
teṣāṃ jñānī nityayukta ekabhaktirviśiṣyate
priyo hi jñānino'tyarthamahaṃ sa ca mama priyaḥ
verses.essence: Of these, the knower — ever harnessed, devoted to the One alone — excels. For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and the knower is dear to me.
verses.translation: Of them the wise, ever steadfast and devoted to the One, excels (is the best); for I am exceedingly dear to the wise and he is dear to Me.

anvaya.parts: नित्य (always) + युक्त (yoked, steadfast): always united
एक (one) + भक्ति (devotion): one whose devotion is to one alone

anvaya.form: verb, present, passive, 3rd person singular (is distinguished)

anvaya.parts: अति (beyond) + अर्थ (measure): beyond all measure

verses.explanation: The ranking, and its reason is not merit but love: eka-bhakti, devotion with one object only, because the jñānī has nothing left to ask the Divine *for* — the Divine has become the point. And then the line that humanizes the Absolute: priyo hi... aham, sa ca mama priyaḥ — I am dear to him; he is dear to *me*. The current runs both ways.
verses.connection: Crowns 7.16's four: when need falls away, what remains between soul and God is affection.
verses.reflection: Love the highest today for no reason at all — drop one 'because' from your devotion.
verses.background: Krishna has just named four kinds of good people who worship him: the troubled, the curious, the seekers of gain and the wise. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as saying which of the four is best, and for what reasons.
verses.hook: Of the four kinds of devotees, which one excels, and why?

views.text: The Self is dear to everyone; since Vāsudeva is the knower's own Self, He is dear to him, and the knower, being the very Self of Vāsudeva, is dear to Him.

Atyartham means beyond words: even the omniscient Lord cannot say how dear He is to the knower, as with Prahlāda, who felt no pain from serpent bites while absorbed in Kṛṣṇa; and He returns that love without limit.
Free of body-identification, the knower has no scattering of mind, so constant union and single devotion are possible for him alone; for these four reasons he is the best.
Those who came in distress, curiosity or desire gradually purify their hearts and grow into selfless, exclusive, constant devotion, unmoved by gain or loss; such devotees are dearest to God.

verses.devanagari:
उदाराः सर्व एवैते ज्ञानी त्वात्मैव मे मतम् ।
आस्थितः स हि युक्तात्मा मामेवानुत्तमां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
udārāḥ sarva evaite jñānī tvātmaiva me matam
āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā māmevānuttamāṃ gatim
verses.essence: Noble are they all — but the knower I hold to be my very Self. For that one, harnessed, abides in me as the highest goal.
verses.translation: Noble indeed are all these; but I deem the wise man as My very Self; for, steadfast in mind he is established in Me alone as the supreme goal.

anvaya.base: आ + √स्था · to stand on, resort to
युक्त-आत्मन् · one whose self is united
anvaya.parts: युक्त (united, steady) + आत्मन् (self, mind): one whose mind is steadfast
अन् (not) + उत्तम (highest): that than which nothing is higher

verses.explanation: First the courtesy — udārāḥ sarva eva, all four are noble, none dismissed — then the staggering elevation: ātmaiva me, the knower is *my own Self*. Not servant, not even friend: the separation itself has worn through. When a being wants nothing but God, God ceases to count that being as other.
verses.connection: Pushes 7.17's mutual love to identity — the chapter's quiet peak of intimacy.
verses.reflection: Pick one act today and do it with the highest as its only goal, no side aim, and notice whether the mind stays steady.
verses.background: Krishna has set the wise worshipper above the other three. Śrīdhara voices the worry this raises: are the other three, then, left out or not dear to him? Krishna answers that, and then says how close the wise one stands to him.
verses.hook: Are all devotees noble, and which one does Krishna regard as his own self?

refs.note: Contrasts lust, which seeks one's own pleasure, with divine love, which seeks only Krishna's happiness, the selfless love of the wise devotee.
Defines true love as finding happiness in the Beloved's happiness, the standard the wise devotee reaches.
Krishna says he becomes bought by devotees who sing his names and keep him close, showing how selfless love binds God.

views.text: No devotee is disagreeable to the Lord, but the knower is not different from Him: his mind rests in 'I am Vāsudeva and none else', and he is going to the supreme Brahman.
All are generous, since the Lord counts even small requests as gifts to Him; the knower is His 'self' because the Lord cannot sustain Himself without him, as the knower cannot live without the Lord.
The other three are not left in saṃsāra: they are great and destined for liberation. The knower is set apart because he takes no fruit other than the Lord.
Every devotee is fortunate, whatever the motive, but the wise love God without wanting anything back; such selfless love binds God so fully that he regards them as himself.

verses.devanagari:
बहूनां जन्मनामन्ते ज्ञानवान्मां प्रपद्यते ।
वासुदेवः सर्वमिति स महात्मा सुदुर्लभः॥
verses.transliteration:
bahūnāṃ janmanāmante jñānavānmāṃ prapadyate
vāsudevaḥ sarvamiti sa mahātmā sudurlabhaḥ
verses.essence: At the end of many births, the one of knowledge takes refuge in me, realizing 'Vasudeva is all there is.' Such a great soul is exceedingly rare.
verses.translation: At the end of many births the wise man comes to Me, realising that all this is Vaasudeva (the innermost Self); such a great soul (Mahatma) is very hard to find.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)

anvaya.base: प्र + √पद् · to go to, resort to

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: महत् (great) + आत्मन् (self): one whose soul is great
सु (very) + दुर्लभ (hard to obtain): extremely rare

verses.explanation: The timeline of the jñānī's arrival: bahūnāṃ janmanām ante, lifetimes of seeking, refining, exhausting every partial answer, until the recognition that cannot be taught dawns whole: vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti, *this*, all of it, is He. Three words that end the search because they leave nowhere outside Him to search. The price is lifetimes, and the commentaries do not discount it: this sentence is not adopted but arrived at. Sa mahātmā sudurlabhaḥ: Śaṅkara reads it as knowledge in its final form, Rāmānuja as the soul's total dependence on Vāsudeva; both call such a soul the rarest of all.
verses.connection: Gives 7.17–18's knower his biography — and the mantra in which all knowing terminates.
verses.reflection: Practice the rare sentence once today, looking at anything: Vasudeva is all this.
verses.background: Krishna has called the wise worshipper his very self. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as praising that person once more. Krishna now tells how such a person arrives, at the end of a long series of lives, and how rarely one is found.
verses.hook: Where does a lifetime of seeking true knowledge finally lead?

refs.note: Without knowledge there is no faith, and without faith love cannot grow, showing that mature knowledge leads to devotion.

views.text: After many births in which the tendencies toward knowledge accumulate, the mature knower directly reaches Vāsudeva as the inmost Self, seeing Him as the Self of all; none equals him.

'Vāsudeva is all' means: He alone is my goal, my means and whatever else I desire, since all beings depend on Him for essence, existence and activity; the reading deliberately excludes a purely monistic sense.
Merit gathers little by little over many births; in the last, the knower worships Me seeing all that moves and does not move as Vāsudeva. His vision is unbounded.
Real knowledge does not look down on devotion; it matures into it. As knowing a ring's true value deepens love for it, the wise after many lives see God as all and surrender.

verses.devanagari:
कामैस्तैस्तैर्हृतज्ञानाः प्रपद्यन्तेऽन्यदेवताः ।
तं तं नियममास्थाय प्रकृत्या नियताः स्वया॥
verses.transliteration:
kāmaistaistairhṛtajñānāḥ prapadyante'nyadevatāḥ
taṃ taṃ niyamamāsthāya prakṛtyā niyatāḥ svayā
verses.essence: Those whose discernment is carried off by this or that desire resort to other deities, following this or that rite, constrained by their own natures.
verses.translation: Those whose wisdom has been rent away by this or that desire, go to other gods, following this or that rite, led by their own nature.

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, instrumental plural (by); repeated to mean 'various'

anvaya.parts: हृत (seized, carried away) + ज्ञान (knowledge): those whose wisdom has been taken

anvaya.base: प्र + √पद् · to go to, resort to

anvaya.parts: अन्य (other) + देवता (deity): deities other than Me

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, accusative singular; repeated to mean 'each relevant'

verses.explanation: The mirror of 7.19: where the knower's vision gathers everything into One, desire splinters vision into many — each want hiring the deity of its department. The verdict is diagnostic, not sneering: prakṛtyā niyatāḥ svayā, steered by their own natures. People worship at the altitude their longings allow.
verses.connection: Returns from the rare summit to the common landscape: why most worship remains plural and transactional.
verses.reflection: Audit your altars honestly: which of your worships were designed by your appetites?
verses.background: Śrīdhara explains the turn: even people with desires who worship Krishna to gain them are slowly freed. Now Krishna speaks of those carried away by desire who turn instead to lesser deities. This verse begins four on such worship.
verses.hook: Why do some people turn to other gods instead of the Supreme?

views.text: Desires for progeny, cattle or heaven take away discrimination; driven by tendencies gathered in past lives, people turn to deities other than Vāsudeva, the Self, with the rites proper to each.
Those who seek even their desires from the Supreme Lord are slowly freed; the intensely rajasic and tamasic, worshipping petty spirits and yakṣas for sons, fame or victory, stay in saṃsāra.
Material desires cloud their understanding, so people worship celestial gods who hold delegated posts, can grant only material things, and cannot free anyone from birth and death.

verses.devanagari:
यो यो यां यां तनुं भक्तः श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति ।
तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yo yo yāṃ yāṃ tanuṃ bhaktaḥ śraddhayārcitumicchati
tasya tasyācalāṃ śraddhāṃ tāmeva vidadhāmyaham
verses.essence: Whatever form a devotee seeks to worship with faith, that very faith I make firm and unwavering.
verses.translation: Whatsoever form any devotee desires to worship with faith that (same) faith of his I make firm and unflinching.

adjective, feminine, accusative singular, goes with श्रद्धाम्

verses.explanation: A theological astonishment hiding in administrative language: when anyone, anywhere, kindles faith toward any form — that flame is steadied *by him*. He underwrites the devotions of his apparent rivals; the God people bypass is the one keeping their bypass lit. Generosity at this depth has stopped keeping score.
verses.connection: Deepens 4.11's 'as they approach me' — even the detour's fuel is supplied by the destination.
verses.reflection: Notice one faith that steadies you today, yours or another's, and consider that the verse says its firmness is given, not self-made.
verses.background: Krishna has described people led by their desires to worship other gods by those gods' own rites. He now explains what part he himself plays in that worship. The verse is about the worshipper's faith, before the next verse turns to the reward.

views.text: Reads the worshipper as a person driven by desire, acting from his own nature; the Lord simply strengthens the very faith he already has, without praising that worship.

Indra and the other deities are the Lord's body, as the inner-controller passage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka teaches; even without knowing this, the worshipper's faith is counted as aimed at Him, and He clears it of obstacles.
Takes 'form' (tanu) to mean a deity, and says the faith steadied by the indwelling Lord comes from impressions left by the worshipper's previous birth.
Only the Supreme Soul within can create faith; he steadies faith even in lesser gods, as parents encourage a child's play with dolls, knowing it helps the soul grow toward him.

verses.hook: Who makes a worshipper's faith firm, whatever form they worship?

verses.devanagari:

लभते च ततः कामान्मयैव विहितान्हि तान्॥

verses.essence: Endowed with that faith, one worships that form and obtains one's desires from it — though in truth they are dispensed by me alone.
verses.translation: Endowed with that faith, he engages in the worship of that (form) and from it he obtains his desire, these being verily ordained by Me (alone).

verses.explanation: The supply chain behind every answered prayer: the worship goes to the chosen counter, the request is filled — mayaiva vihitān, from his warehouse, always. No deity is an independent vendor; all granting routes through the one Granter. The system works precisely because its many faces share a single treasury.
verses.connection: Completes 7.21's mechanics: faith steadied by him, fruits delivered by him — the middle gods are windows.
verses.reflection: Receive one answered wish today knowing who the real treasurer was.
verses.background: Krishna has said he steadies the faith of each worshipper, whatever god they choose. This verse follows that faith through to its result: the worshipper performs the rites, and the desires they asked for arrive. Krishna tells where those results really come from.

views.text: The fruits are certain because the omniscient Lord alone knows how results are apportioned to actions. Notes a variant reading hitān ('beneficial') for hi tān, which must then be taken figuratively, since desires benefit no one.
Because Indra and the others are the Lord's body, their worship is in fact His worship, even though the worshipper does not know it, so the fruit is granted by Him alone.
Those who chase such finite rewards lack discrimination: they pick up pieces of glass instead of the priceless jewel of the Self.
Celestial gods cannot fulfil desires on their own; they grant wishes only as God permits, so whatever the worshipper obtains is really arranged by God.

verses.hook: When worship of a lesser deity bears fruit, who really grants it?

verses.devanagari:
अन्तवत्तु फलं तेषां तद्भवत्यल्पमेधसाम् ।
देवान्देवयजो यान्ति मद्भक्ता यान्ति मामपि॥

verses.essence: But finite is the fruit of those of small understanding. Worshipers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
verses.translation: Verily the reward (fruit) that accrues to those men of small intelligence is finite. The worshippers of the gods go to them, but My devotees come to Me.

verses.explanation: The honest price-tag on 7.21–22's generosity: antavat, the lesser counters pay in perishable coin — health, wealth, heavens with expiry dates. The law beneath it is destination-by-orientation: you arrive at what you aimed at. Aim at the limited and receive it, fully; aim at the Unlimited and receive *that*. The tragedy of small prayers is not that they fail but that they succeed.
verses.connection: The fine print after the open-handedness: every worship works, and each delivers exactly its own size.
verses.reflection: Aim today at the source, not the perks — finite worship buys finite goods.
verses.background: Krishna has said the worshippers of other gods do get what they ask, though he himself grants it. Śrīdhara explains the point now made: even if every god is his own form, the result differs for those who worship him directly. This verse weighs the two rewards.

views.text: The effort is the same either way, yet people do not turn to the Lord for the unlimited result; the verse is His expression of compassion for their pitiable state.
The gods' joy and lifespan are limited, so those who reach them fall with them in time; His devotees, who give up finite fruits, reach Him and never return to saṃsāra (citing 8.16).
The deity such people worship carries only an 'intermediate body' of the Lord shaped to their desires; the result comes from Him but ends, because it is bounded by their own mental impressions.
Ranks the worship of lesser beings: Indra and the gods by sattvic devotees, yakṣas and rākṣasas by rajasic ones, ghosts and spirits by tamasic ones; none of it leads to liberation.
One reaches what one worships: worshippers of perishable gods get perishable rewards and their realms, as students leave primary school behind; devotees of the eternal God reach his eternal abode.

verses.hook: Where do worshippers of the gods go, and where do Krishna's devotees go?

अव्यक्तं व्यक्तिमापन्नं मन्यन्ते मामबुद्धयः ।

verses.translation: The foolish think of Me, the Unmanifest, as having manifestation, knowing not My higher, immutable and most excellent nature.

verses.explanation: The subtlest error in the chapter: taking the visible Krishna as the whole of Krishna — a prince born by karma like anyone else, someone who was not there before and has only now appeared. The correction: the form is real, but behind it stands paraṁ bhāvam, an unmanifest supremacy the eyes never exhaust. The error is not seeing him; it is concluding that what is seen is all there is.
verses.connection: Opens the hiddenness verses (7.24–26): the foolish take the Unmanifest for a merely visible form, an error 7.25 traces to Krishna's veiling power.
verses.reflection: Catch yourself shrinking the infinite to its visible form today — honor the door, seek the dwelling.
verses.background: Krishna has just contrasted lasting and passing rewards. Śrīdhara asks: if the effort is the same and the reward so much greater, why do not all worship him? This verse gives the reason, in how people misjudge what Krishna is.

views.text: The unintelligent, unaware of His reality as the supreme Self, suppose that the ever-existing God has only now become visible by taking an embodied incarnation.

They miss that the Lord of all took birth as Vasudeva's son without giving up His divine nature, out of compassion, so that all could take refuge in Him; seeing only a prince, they neither resort to Him nor worship Him.
Such worshippers grasp only a manifest form suited to their own desires, which is why no single name or form is insisted on; a form held fast in order to be rid of desires itself purifies and frees.
His human, fish and tortoise forms are bodies of pure sattva shown in play to protect the world; the dull see a karma-made body like any other god's and turn to deities that give quick fruit.

God's divine personal form is eternal and primordial, not something born from the formless Brahman, which is the light it radiates; neither aspect is higher, though the personal form reveals his qualities openly.

verses.hook: Did God's personal form arise from a formless source?

refs.note: Says the light from the toenails of God's personal form is what knowers worship as the formless Brahman, supporting the personal form as primary.

verses.devanagari:
नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः ।
मूढोऽयं नाभिजानाति लोको मामजमव्ययम्॥
verses.transliteration:
nāhaṃ prakāśaḥ sarvasya yogamāyāsamāvṛtaḥ
mūḍho'yaṃ nābhijānāti loko māmajamavyayam
verses.essence: Veiled by my yoga-maya, I am not revealed to all. This deluded world does not recognize me — unborn, imperishable.
verses.translation: I am not manifest to all (as I am) veiled by the Yoga-Maya. This deluded world does not know Me, the unborn and imperishable.

verses.explanation: Why the error of 7.24 is nearly universal: the concealment is active. Yoga-māyā-samāvṛtaḥ — wrapped in his own power of seeming, the way an actor's role hides the actor most perfectly from those nearest the stage. The hiddenness of God is not distance or absence; it is camouflage worn within the scene.
verses.connection: Explains the veil's operation: 7.13's blindness is also, from his side, a deliberate discretion.
verses.reflection: Notice one moment today when the world's surface fully absorbs you, and recall that the verse calls this a veil, not all that is there.
verses.background: Krishna has said the foolish take him for no more than a visible being, not knowing his higher nature. Śaṅkara asks what causes this ignorance. Krishna names the veil that hides him.

views.text: Yoga here is the coming together of the three guṇas, and that is māyā. Being His own, it veils Him from the world but not His own knowledge, as magic never fools the magician; He is manifest only to some devotees.
The veil is the human form He takes; the foolish see only that and miss that He, unborn and Lord of all, took it so that everyone who wants can take refuge in Him.
Yoga is His inconceivable play of wisdom, and māyā is His skill in bringing about the impossible; covered by it, He is plain only to His devotees.
Yogmaya, God's highest energy, hides his divinity from those not yet eligible and by grace reveals him to the surrendered; her forms such as Radha and Sita are revered as the Divine Mother.

verses.hook: Why is God not visible to everyone, even when he is present?

refs.note: Names three chief energies of Vishnu, the higher one, the souls, and the energy of ignorance and action, introducing Yogmaya as distinct.
Says God's form is divine and only the pure in heart know it by his grace, supporting Yogmaya's veiling and revealing.

verses.devanagari:
वेदाहं समतीतानि वर्तमानानि चार्जुन ।
भविष्याणि च भूतानि मां तु वेद न कश्चन॥

bhaviṣyāṇi ca bhūtāni māṃ tu veda na kaścana
verses.essence: I know the beings of the past, the present and the future, Arjuna — but no one knows me.
verses.translation: I know, O Arjuna, the beings of the past, the present and the future, but no one knows Me.

verses.explanation: The asymmetry of knowledge, drawn absolutely: every being across all three times stands transparent before him; he stands opaque before every being. The mirror sees the room; the room cannot see into the mirror. Said by anyone else, vanity — said from the position 7.24–25 described, simple geometry.
verses.connection: Caps the hiddenness verses with their starkest formulation — total knower, totally unknown.
verses.reflection: Rest in the asymmetry today: fully known by what you cannot corner. Let yourself be the known one.
verses.background: Krishna has said that his power of illusion hides him from the world. Śaṅkara adds that this power, being his own, does not hide anything from him, as a magician is not fooled by his own trick. Krishna now states what he knows and what others do not.

views.text: Apart from the devotee who has taken refuge in Him, no one adores Him, simply because no one knows His reality.
Of all the beings He looks after across the three times, none understands Him as Vasudeva come to be everyone's refuge; that is why the true knower is so hard to find.
He knows all because māyā rests on Him and does not delude its own support, while it deludes everyone else, as a conjurer's illusion fools the audience but not the conjurer.
God knows every soul's thoughts and deeds across lifetimes and keeps the karmic record, but our finite intellect cannot grasp him; he is known only when he grants his grace.

verses.hook: Can anyone know God the way God knows all beings?

refs.note: Describes God as all-knowing, his austerity made of knowledge, matching his knowledge of past, present and future beings.
Says this understanding cannot be reached by reasoning, supporting that no one knows God by intellect.
Words turn back from God together with the mind, failing to reach him, so he exceeds all comprehension.

verses.devanagari:
इच्छाद्वेषसमुत्थेन द्वन्द्वमोहेन भारत ।
सर्वभूतानि सम्मोहं सर्गे यान्ति परन्तप॥
verses.transliteration:
icchādveṣasamutthena dvandvamohena bhārata
sarvabhūtāni sammohaṃ sarge yānti parantapa

verses.translation: By the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, O Bharata, all beings are subject to delusion at birth, O Parantapa.

verses.explanation: The mechanics of the universal blindness: icchā and dveṣa — want and recoil — generate the pairs, and the pairs (pleasant-unpleasant, gain-loss, mine-yours) form the lens every newborn perceives through, sarge, from the very start. No one *falls* into delusion; everyone arrives pre-fitted with it. Which makes the next verse's exit all the more precious.
verses.connection: Traces 7.25–26's unknowing to its engine: the sorting reflex installed before the first memory.
verses.reflection: Watch the pull-push trance for one hour — every like and dislike a thread of the birth-veil.
verses.background: Krishna has said that he knows all beings but none know him. Śaṅkara has him anticipate the question: what blocks beings from knowing him from the moment they are born? This verse names that block.

views.text: Likes and dislikes take over the intellect; if even plain knowledge of outer things fails under them, knowledge of the inner Self cannot arise. Every creature is born already gripped by this delusion.
Impressions from past births make love and hate for pleasant and painful things instinctive from birth; only the knower is born with joy in union with the Lord and pain in separation from Him.
Takes the verse cosmically: in dissolution beings lie as if asleep inside Prakṛti, still holding their impressions, so no liberation comes, and when they wake the round of worldly life starts again.
Sarga means the birth of the gross body; liking and aversion toward what suits it breed the deep conviction 'I am happy, I am miserable', which keeps beings from knowing the Lord.
Attraction and aversion to life's pairs, pleasure and pain, birth and death, come from ignorance; adversity can lift the soul, and the wise accept dualities as part of God's creation.

verses.hook: Why are all beings caught in confusion from the moment of birth?

verses.devanagari:
येषां त्वन्तगतं पापं जनानां पुण्यकर्मणाम् ।
ते द्वन्द्वमोहनिर्मुक्ता भजन्ते मां दृढव्रताः॥
verses.transliteration:
yeṣāṃ tvantagataṃ pāpaṃ janānāṃ puṇyakarmaṇām
te dvandvamohanirmuktā bhajante māṃ dṛḍhavratāḥ

verses.translation: But those men of virtuous deeds whose sins have come to an end, and who are freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship Me, steadfast in their vows.

verses.explanation: The exit from 7.27's congenital fog, and its sequence matters: anta-gataṁ pāpam — accumulated wrong worn down by lives of clean action — *then* the lens of the pairs loosens, *then* worship becomes dṛḍha-vrata, steady. Purity is not the reward of vision; it is vision's prerequisite. Conduct clears the windshield that doctrine alone cannot.
verses.connection: Answers 7.27: the fog is congenital but not permanent — washed thin by lived goodness.
verses.reflection: Do one clean deed today and feel it thin the lens — ethics is optics here.
verses.background: Krishna has said that all beings are born into delusion. Śrīdhara asks the obvious question: then how is it that some people are seen worshipping you? Krishna describes those people and what has freed them.

views.text: Sin is 'come to an end' in the sense of nearly worn away by virtuous deeds that purify the mind; 'firm in vow' means holding the firm knowledge that the supreme Reality is just this and not otherwise.

Sins piled up since beginningless time, which breed attraction and aversion and turn one from the Lord, are weakened by good actions over many births; such people then worship Him, each in the way their merit allows.
'Firm in vow' means single-minded (ekāntin); once every obstructing sin is destroyed and the delusion of the pairs is gone, they worship the Lord alone.
Those freed from desire and hatred worship God with firm resolve; they seek no pleasure in the world, avoid what deludes, and treat hardship as a chance to grow.

verses.hook: Who become free enough from likes and dislikes to worship God steadily?

verses.explanation: The chapter begins its handover: those who flee the two unanswerables — aging and death — by fleeing *to him* are promised the whole curriculum: Brahman, adhyātma and karma, each known kṛtsnam, entire. Refuge turns out to be the fastest scholarship; what the mind chases for lifetimes, surrender is simply handed.
verses.connection: Takes up 7.14's refuge again: those who take refuge in Krishna strive past old age and death, and come to know the supreme reality, the self and action.
verses.reflection: Let even the plain wish not to be erased drive your practice today — that root is honored.
verses.background: Krishna has described the good people, freed from the pull of opposites, who worship him firmly. Śaṅkara asks why they worship, and this verse answers. Krishna names their aim and what they come to know, introducing terms Arjuna will soon ask him to explain.

views.text: Taking refuge in God means keeping the mind absorbed in him; those who so strive for freedom from old age and death know the supreme Brahman, everything about the indwelling individual Self, and all action.
These are seekers of kaivalya, the self's isolation in its own bliss; 'Brahman' here means the pure individual self seen as distinct from Prakṛti, not the supreme Lord.
They know the supreme Brahman, the pure self distinct from the body as what is to be attained, and the whole of karma with its secret as the means to it, and so reach fulfilment.
Such people realise that all is Vāsudeva and that there is no real diversity; they are not reborn and are liberated here and now.
Though intellect cannot know God, the surrendered receive his grace, and with it knowledge of God, of the self and of karma; self-knowledge is only a drop beside knowledge of God.

verses.hook: What do those who seek freedom from old age and death come to know?

refs.note: Says the Self is not gained by discourse, intellect or much learning, but only by the one he chooses, to whom he reveals himself; so knowledge comes by grace.
Teach that when the One is known, everything becomes known, as those sheltered in God receive full knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
साधिभूताधिदैवं मां साधियज्ञं च ये विदुः ।
प्रयाणकालेऽपि च मां ते विदुर्युक्तचेतसः॥
verses.transliteration:

verses.translation: Those who know Me with the Adhibhuta (pertaining to the elements), Adhidaiva (pertaining to the gods) and the Adhiyajna (pertaining to the sacrifice) know Me even at the time of death, steadfast in mind.

verses.explanation: The chapter closes mid-sentence, deliberately: three technical terms dropped without definition, and one phrase that changes the conversation's gravity — prayāṇa-kāle, at the time of going forth. To know him so thoroughly that even dying does not dislodge the knowing: that is the final examination, and chapter 8 will be its study guide.
verses.connection: Arjuna's seven questions in 8.1–2 come straight from 7.29–30: the six terms in the order Krishna named them, then the hour of death.
verses.reflection: Hold one truth firmly enough today that you could hold it at the hour of departure.
verses.background: Chapter 7 closes here. Krishna adds three more terms to those he has just named, and carries what such worshippers know through to the hour of death. Śrīdhara introduces it as removing any fear that such people might lose their yoga, and notes that Krishna will explain the new terms in the next chapter.

views.text: Those who know Brahman in every setting, the individual, action, the physical, the divine and the sacrificial, never lose awareness of It, not even at the critical moment of death.

The repeated 'those' marks a further group, seekers of power; knowing Him as connected with sacrifice is enjoined on all three kinds of aspirant, and each knows Him at death in keeping with his own goal.
Those who have remembered the Lord ever since birth will surely remember Him at the last moment, so the question 'why worship from birth onward?' deserves only silence.
The Lord will define adhibhūta and the rest in the next chapter; the point here is that His devotees need not fear falling from yoga, since even when dying they do not panic and forget Him.
Death's pain usually overwhelms mind and intellect, but those whose mind is wholly given to God are beyond bodily consciousness and stay aware of him at the end, reaching his abode.

verses.hook: Who can still remember God at the moment of death?
